title: Auxiliary Power Unit Slow to Accept Load at High Field Elevation — Kalahari Express
abstract: Kalahari Express reports that at its high-elevation bases the auxiliary power unit takes far longer than expected to accept the air load, delaying pushback and forcing ground carts to stay connected past the scheduled off-blocks time.

sections.request: At our two highland stations the APU will start and run but it will not take the air load for a long time after that. The crews see the availability indication come up and then wait, sometimes three or four minutes, before they can close the doors and get the packs on the unit. On a tight turnaround that is the whole margin. Our ground handling contract charges us when the air cart stays connected past the slot, so this is costing money on every rotation, not just occasionally. At sea level stations we do not see it at all. We would like the unit to be usable at these fields on the same timeline as everywhere else.
sections.background: We raised this through the technical account meeting in late 2025 and were advised it was within specification for the altitude. Our own trend data covers two hundred and forty starts at the affected fields and shows a median delay of two minutes fifty against a sea level median of forty seconds. There is no correlation with unit hours or with which airframe. Two ground carts have been damaged by extended running in the heat, which is a separate cost we are carrying.
sections.expected_outcome: A predictable time from availability to load acceptance at field elevations above two thousand metres, close enough to the sea level figure that we can build it into the turnaround plan. If the behaviour is protective we need it written down so our crews stop reporting it as a fault.

type_data.business_justification: Ground handling penalties on roughly four hundred rotations a year at two stations, plus two damaged air carts. The operator puts the recurring cost at 310 kEUR a year and rising with the winter schedule expansion.
